hook: Your bank pays you 0.01% and lends your money out at 7%. That gap has a name: their profit.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A bank account built for holding money rather than spending it. No debit card for purchases, usually a limit on how many withdrawals per month, and it pays interest: the bank pays you a small percentage for leaving money there.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone keeping money aside for a goal or an emergency. Most people's first one is at the same bank as their checking.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The bank lends your deposits out at a much higher rate than it pays you. The FDIC's national average savings rate was 0.38% in August 2026, many large banks paid 0.01%, and competitive online accounts paid around 4%. That gap is the bank's profit.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Earning almost nothing without realizing better options exist. Monthly fees on some accounts if the balance drops.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the APY? Is there a minimum balance or a fee? How fast can I move money back to checking?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Same savings account. Ten to fifty times the interest. The difference is a building.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A savings account that pays a much higher interest rate, often 10 to 50 times a traditional bank's rate. Usually offered by online-only banks that have no branches to pay for.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: People holding an emergency fund or saving for something within the next few years who want the money to earn something while staying safe and reachable.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Same model as any bank, with a smaller cut. The rate is also a marketing tool: it moves with the Federal Reserve's rates and some banks trim it quietly once you've moved money in.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: The rate is variable and can drop. Transfers to your main bank can take 1 to 3 business days. Some accounts have tiers or caps on what earns the headline rate.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is this FDIC insured? Is the rate the same on the whole balance, or only up to a cap? How long do transfers take? Has this bank's rate held up over the last year?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Two accounts, same rate, different earnings. The letter that explains it is Y.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: The interest rate is the plain percentage. APY (annual percentage yield) is what you actually earn in a year once interest is paid on interest, called compounding. APY is always equal to or slightly higher than the rate. For borrowing, the equivalent number is APR, which has its own card.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone comparing two savings accounts or CDs. APY is the number that lets you compare apples to apples.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Marketing. Ads lead with whichever number looks better. For savings they show APY (bigger); for loans they'd rather you not look at APR at all.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Comparing one account's rate to another's APY and picking wrong. Also mistaking a short promotional APY for the ongoing one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is this number APY or rate? Is it promotional, and for how long? What's the APY after the promo ends?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The logo on the app is not the same as the guarantee on your money.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A government guarantee that if your bank fails, you get your money back, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per account category. Credit unions have the same thing under a different name (NCUA). It covers deposits like checking, savings, and CDs. It does not cover investments.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Everyone with a bank account, automatically, as long as the bank is a member. Nearly all U.S. banks are.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: It doesn't. Banks pay premiums into the fund. The thing to watch is companies that aren't banks (some fintech apps, some crypto platforms) using the FDIC logo loosely. Their coverage, if any, runs through a partner bank and can have gaps.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Assuming an app is a bank. Keeping more than $250,000 at one bank in one name. Confusing "FDIC insured" (deposits) with "SIPC" (brokerage accounts, which protect against the broker failing, not against investments losing value).

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is this company itself an FDIC-insured bank, or does it hold my money at a partner bank? Which partner? Does coverage apply if the app, not the bank, goes under?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Insurance is the one thing you buy hoping to never use.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: You pay a premium each month, and if a covered bad thing happens, the insurer pays for it, after you pay the deductible. Health, auto, renters or homeowners, and term life are the ones most people need at some point. Each has a limit on what it pays and a list of what it doesn't cover.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Health: nearly everyone. Auto: required by every state and every lender. Renters: anyone renting, and it's cheap. Term life: people with someone who depends on their income.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Premiums are priced so that, across all customers, the insurer takes in more than it pays out. Riders, low deductibles, and add-ons raise the premium more than they raise the coverage. Whole life and other investment-style policies carry high commissions, which is why they're sold hard.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Being underinsured on the big things (liability, health) and overinsured on the small ones (phone, extended warranties). Not knowing the deductible until the claim. Letting a policy lapse and finding out the gap isn't covered.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the deductible and what's the maximum it pays? What specifically is excluded? Is this term or permanent life insurance, and why? What does the same coverage cost from two other companies?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: You have several credit scores, not one, and three companies sell them.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A three-digit number, usually 300 to 850, that lenders use to guess how likely you are to pay back what you borrow. Built from your history: whether you pay on time, how much of your available credit you use, how long you've had accounts, and how often you apply for new ones. The most common versions are FICO and VantageScore, and you have several scores, not one.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone who will ever rent an apartment, get a phone plan, finance a car, or take a mortgage. Employers and insurers sometimes check it too.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) sell your data to lenders. "Free credit score" apps are usually paid by the cards and loans they show you next to your score. Paid "credit monitoring" is often selling what you can get free by law.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: A low score makes every loan cost more, sometimes for years. Errors on your report are common and are yours to dispute. Checking your own score does not hurt it; a lender's "hard pull" when you apply does, a little.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Which score is this (FICO? Vantage? which version)? What's dragging it down: late payments, high utilization, short history? When did I last pull my free reports from the three bureaus?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The minimum payment is a number designed to keep you paying.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: The arithmetic of getting out of debt. Two numbers decide it: the rate and how much more than the minimum you pay. At a 22% card rate, paying only the minimum on a balance can take well over a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchases. Every card statement is required to show you this calculation.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone carrying a balance on more than one thing: cards, a BNPL plan, a car, a student loan. The question is which to pay down first.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Lenders earn on the balance, so the longer it lasts the more they make. The minimum payment is set low enough to keep the balance alive for years. Debt-relief companies charge fees for plans you can usually set up yourself.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Paying extra on the lowest-rate loan first. Consolidating into a new loan and then running the cards back up. Not noticing a 0% promo ending and interest charging back from day one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the rate on each balance? What's the minimum on each, and what happens if I put the extra on the highest rate first versus the smallest balance first? How long does the statement say this balance takes at the minimum?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The minimum payment is set exactly where it is for a reason. The reason is not you.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A card that lets you borrow from the card company each time you buy something. You get a bill once a month. Pay the full balance by the due date and you pay no interest. Pay less than that and interest starts on what's left, at a rate that's usually among the highest of any common loan.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Most adults. Used in full each month, it's a convenient way to pay that builds credit history and sometimes earns rewards. Used as a loan, it's expensive.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Three ways: interest on balances you carry (the big one), a fee the store pays on every swipe (which funds rewards), and annual or late fees. Rewards programs are designed to work only if you spend more, and they're funded by people who carry balances.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: The minimum payment. It's set low enough that a balance can take years and cost more in interest than the original purchase. Also: a card is not an emergency fund, though it gets used as one.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the APR, and is there a different one for cash advances? Is there an annual fee? What's the grace period? If I only paid the minimum, how long would this balance take to clear (the statement has to tell you)?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Most people with a card balance can't name their APR within ten points.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Annual percentage rate: the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage. It's the borrowing twin of APY. The average rate on cards that carried a balance was about 22% in August 2026. At 24%, a $1,000 balance carried for a year costs roughly $240 in interest, charged a bit each day. Loans with fees fold those fees into APR, which is why APR is the number to compare across lenders.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone with a card, a car loan, a mortgage, a student loan, or a BNPL plan. It's on every one of them, by law.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: It is how they make money. The trick is where it's shown: big for the 0% promo, small for what comes after. "Variable" APR means it moves when the Federal Reserve moves rates, which is most cards.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Not knowing yours. Promotional 0% periods that end and sometimes charge back interest from day one ("deferred interest") if any balance remains.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the APR after any promo? Fixed or variable? Is this "0% APR" or "no interest if paid in full," which is a different and worse thing?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Four easy payments. The store pays the fee. So who's the product?

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Splitting a purchase into a few payments, typically four over six weeks, offered at checkout by companies like Affirm, Klarna, and Afterpay, and increasingly by card issuers themselves. The short "pay in 4" plans usually charge no interest. Longer plans for bigger purchases often do.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Online shoppers, heavily under 35, and increasingly for groceries and everyday items, which is what regulators watch.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The store pays the BNPL company a fee (often 2 to 8% of the sale) for the extra sales it drives. You pay late fees if you miss an installment, and interest on the longer plans. The business model depends on people buying more than they would have with one payment.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Stacking: four or five plans running at once across different apps, with no single bill. Affirm began reporting all its plans to Experian in April 2025, and FICO released score versions that include BNPL data in late 2025, so these plans are starting to show up on credit files. Returns and refunds get messy when the merchant and the lender are different companies.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is this plan 0%, and what's the APR if not? What's the late fee? Does this report to credit bureaus, and does paying on time help or only hurt? How many of these do I have open right now?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The loan you signed at 18 has two versions, and the difference is thousands of dollars.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Money borrowed for school. Federal loans come from the government with a fixed rate set each year (6.52% for undergraduates in 2026-27), income-based repayment options, and no credit check. Private loans come from banks, with rates set by your credit and fewer ways out if things go wrong.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: About half of people who finish a four-year degree, and plenty who don't finish. Parents too, through PLUS loans, which carry the highest federal rate.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Interest. On an unsubsidized loan it starts accruing the day the money is sent, while you're still in school, and gets added to the balance when repayment begins. Servicers are paid by the government to collect; private lenders keep the spread between what they borrow at and what they charge you.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Not knowing which type you have, because the rules are different. Interest capitalizing during a deferment. Missing that federal loans have income-based plans and private ones usually don't. Refinancing federal loans into private ones and losing those protections for a slightly lower rate.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Are these federal or private? Subsidized or not? What's the rate on each loan, and is interest accruing right now? Who is the servicer, and what repayment plans am I eligible for?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The dealer asks what you can afford per month. That question is the sales tactic.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A loan to buy a vehicle, with the vehicle as collateral: miss payments and it can be repossessed. You pay the price plus interest over a set term. In early 2026 the average new-car loan was about $44,000 at $770 a month over 69 months, and more than a third of new loans ran longer than six years.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Most people who buy a car. Dealers arrange many of these loans on the spot, often through their own lender partners.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Interest, and the term. Stretching a loan from 60 to 84 months lowers the monthly payment and raises the total you pay, which is why the conversation starts with the payment, not the price. Dealers can also earn a markup on the rate they arrange for you, and sell add-ons (warranties, protection plans) rolled into the loan.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Being underwater: owing more than the car is worth for the first few years, which is nearly guaranteed on a long loan with a small down payment. Negotiating the payment instead of the price. Not knowing the rate until the paperwork.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the total price of the car, and what's the APR? What's the term? What would the payment be at a shorter term? Is there a rate from my own bank or credit union to compare against before I sit down?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Part of your salary is sitting in a drawer at HR, and you only get it if you ask.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A 401(k) is a retirement account offered through an employer. Money goes in from your paycheck before it reaches you. A match is when the employer adds its own money on top, usually a formula like "50% of what you put in, up to 6% of your pay" or "100% of the first 3%, then 50% of the next 2%." The match is part of your pay that you only get if you contribute.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Employees whose company offers one. Not every job does, and some require a waiting period before the match kicks in.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The plan provider charges fees, often buried in the funds inside the plan (see Expense ratio). Some plans have good, cheap fund menus; some have bad, expensive ones, and you can't shop around because your employer picked it.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Leaving the match on the table. Not knowing the vesting schedule: the employer's contributions may not fully belong to you until you've stayed a certain number of years. Early withdrawals before 59½ generally mean taxes plus a 10% penalty.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the match formula, exactly? When am I fully vested? What funds are in the plan and what do they cost? Is there a Roth option inside it?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Roth and traditional are not two products. They're one account with two tax calendars.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Two tax treatments that apply to retirement accounts (both 401(k)s and IRAs). Traditional: money goes in before tax, grows untaxed, and you pay income tax when you take it out. Roth: money goes in after tax, grows untaxed, and comes out tax-free. Same account, different timing of the tax. An IRA is the version you open yourself, not through work, with lower annual limits.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone saving for retirement in a tax-advantaged account has to pick one, and the choice turns on tax rates now versus later, which nobody knows for sure.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The accounts themselves don't. Brokerages earn on what's inside them and on cash sitting uninvested. Some providers charge IRA account fees; many charge none.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Thinking it's a product rather than a tax label. Contributing to a Roth IRA when income is above the limit. Treating "tax-free later" as free: Roth contributions cost you the deduction today.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is my income likely higher or lower now than it will be in retirement? What are this year's contribution limits? For 2026 the IRA limit is $7,500 under age 50, and Roth IRA eligibility phases out above $153,000 of income for single filers and $242,000 for joint filers; they change yearly, so check the IRS page. Does my 401(k) offer both?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: One purchase, 500 companies, and nobody getting paid to guess.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A fund that buys a whole list of investments at once, matching an index like the S&P 500 (500 large U.S. companies) rather than trying to pick winners. One purchase gives you a small slice of everything on the list. Comes in two wrappers: a mutual fund (priced once a day) or an ETF (trades like a stock during the day).

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Most first-time investors and a large share of professionals. It's the default inside many 401(k)s and robo-advisors.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The expense ratio, which is small by design, often 0.03 to 0.20% per year. That's the whole pitch: it's cheap because no one is being paid to pick stocks. Some brokers also earn on the cash in your account or on "payment for order flow" when you trade.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: It goes down when the market goes down, fully. There's no manager stepping in. Historically broad markets have recovered, but over years, not weeks, and past results don't guarantee future ones. Also: not all "index funds" track broad indexes; some track narrow or gimmicky ones with higher fees.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What index does it track? What's the expense ratio? Is there a sales charge ("load") or a minimum? Is this a mutual fund or an ETF, and does that matter for how I'd buy it?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: A fee you never see a bill for, charged every year for the rest of your life.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage of what you have in it, taken out automatically so you never see a bill. 0.05% means $5 a year on $10,000. 1.00% means $100. It's the single most reliable predictor of how one fund will do against a similar one, because it's the one thing known in advance.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone holding a fund, whether they know it or not. It's on every fund's fact sheet and in your 401(k) plan documents.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: This is the fee. It's how fund companies, and often the advisor or plan that put you in the fund, get paid. Because it's a percentage, it grows with your balance for the rest of your life.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Compounding against you. Two funds holding similar things at 0.05% and 1.00% can end up tens of thousands of dollars apart over a working life, on the same contributions. Target-date funds and "managed" options in 401(k)s are where high ratios hide most often.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the expense ratio of each fund I'm in? Is there a similar fund in the menu that's cheaper? Are there other fees on top (advisory, administrative, 12b-1)?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The same math that grows a retirement account is the math that grows a card balance.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Earning returns on your returns. Money that grows 7% in year one is a bigger pile in year two, so 7% of that is more dollars, and so on. Over long periods the curve bends upward. It works the same way in reverse on debt: unpaid interest gets added to the balance and then earns interest itself.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Everyone, whether they mean to or not. Savers and investors benefit from it; people carrying card balances are on the other side of it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The idea is free. But it's the engine behind both the expense ratio (a small fee compounding against you for decades) and credit card APR. Anyone selling you something will show compounding working for you and skip where it's working against you.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Expecting it to feel like much in the first few years. It doesn't; the dramatic part comes late, which is why time in the market has mattered more than the size of the first deposit. And mistaking a projection ("at 7% a year") for a promise. Returns are not steady. Broad U.S. stocks have averaged roughly 6.5 to 7% a year after inflation over two centuries, with long stretches well above and below that, and none of it is a guarantee.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What rate is this projection assuming, and is it after fees? Over how many years? What does the same math say about my debt?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The account is free. The broker still gets paid. Here's how.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: An account at a brokerage firm where you can hold and trade investments: stocks, bonds, funds. Unlike a 401(k) or IRA it has no contribution limits and no tax break, so gains are taxed when you sell. Money moves in from your bank, sits as cash until you buy something, and comes out whenever you want.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone investing outside a retirement account, or who has already filled their tax-advantaged ones. Also the account most people open first when they want to try investing.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Even with zero-commission trades: interest on your uninvested cash (they pay you little and lend it out), payment for order flow (market makers pay the broker to execute your trades), margin interest, and fees on the broker's own funds. Free is the price of the account, not of the relationship.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Leaving cash sitting uninvested for months. Trading often because it feels free. Confusing SIPC protection (covers the broker failing) with protection against losses.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What do you pay on uninvested cash? Do you accept payment for order flow? Are there fees to transfer out? Is this account SIPC protected?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: One is owning. The other is lending. Everything else is detail.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A stock is a slice of ownership in a company: you get a share of its profits if it does well and nothing promised if it doesn't. A bond is a loan to a company or government: they pay you a set interest rate and give the money back at the end. Stocks swing more and have historically returned more; bonds swing less and pay less.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Nearly every investment account holds some of each, usually through funds. The mix is what people mean by how risky a portfolio is.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Stocks: the company earns on your money, not off you, but the fund or broker you hold it through charges fees. Bonds: the borrower pays you interest; the middlemen earn on the spread and on fund fees.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Thinking bond prices only go one way (they fall when rates rise). Holding all stocks and selling in the first drop. Holding all bonds for decades and losing ground to inflation.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the mix of stocks and bonds in what I own? How much did a portfolio like this fall in the last bad year? What am I being paid to lend, and to whom?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Same fund, two wrappers. The difference is when you can buy it and what it costs to hold.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Two ways to package the same basket of investments. A mutual fund is bought and sold once a day at that day's closing price, often with a minimum investment. An ETF trades on an exchange all day like a stock, with no minimum beyond one share. Many index funds exist in both forms with the same holdings.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone buying a fund. In a 401(k) you usually get mutual funds; in a brokerage account most people buy ETFs.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The expense ratio either way. Mutual funds sometimes add sales charges (loads) or 12b-1 marketing fees. ETFs cost a bid-ask spread each time you trade. In a taxable account ETFs usually pass on fewer capital gains, which matters at tax time.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Paying a load on a mutual fund when a near-identical ETF has none. Trading an ETF often because you can. Buying an ETF at a thin moment and paying a wide spread.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Is there a sales charge or a minimum? What's the expense ratio for each version? Does this fund distribute capital gains every year? If I'm in a 401(k), which wrapper does the plan actually offer?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The fund that picks itself. Convenient, and where fees most often hide.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A single fund that holds a mix of stocks and bonds and shifts toward bonds as a chosen year (2055, 2060) approaches. You pick the year closest to when you'd retire and it rebalances itself. It's the default option in many 401(k) plans and held $4.8 trillion in 2025.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: People who want one choice and never want to think about it again, and everyone who was auto-enrolled in a 401(k) and never changed the default.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The expense ratio, which averaged 0.27% in 2025 but ranges from under 0.1% to over 0.7% depending on the provider. The fund of funds structure can stack a fee on top of the underlying funds' fees. Compare that to 0.14% for a plain index ETF.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Assuming all target-date funds are cheap. Two funds with the same year can hold very different mixes. Holding one in a brokerage account alongside other funds and ending up with the same thing twice.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the total expense ratio, including the underlying funds? What's the stock/bond mix today and at the target year? Is there a cheaper target-date series in the same plan? Is it built from index funds or actively managed ones?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Every scam has the same three parts. Learn the shape and the version doesn't matter.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Someone getting you to send money or information by pretending to be something they're not. People reported about $16 billion in fraud losses in 2025, a record, with $3.5 billion of that from imposters posing as a bank, a government agency, a company, or a relative. The method changes monthly; the structure doesn't.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Everyone, and increasingly younger adults, who report losing money more often than older ones. Nobody thinks they're the target until they are.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The scam is the product; the whole thing is how it makes money off you. The three parts: a promise or a threat (guaranteed returns, your account is compromised, a relative in trouble), urgency (act now, don't tell anyone), and an untraceable payment (wire, crypto, gift cards, a payment app to a stranger).

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Acting before checking. Trusting caller ID, an email address, or a voice (all can be faked). Sending a second payment to recover the first, which is its own scam. Not reporting it because of embarrassment.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Can I hang up and call the organization back at the number on my card or statement? Why does this need to happen right now? Why this payment method? Would a real bank, agency, or employer ever ask for this?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Your paycheck is lying to you. Not on purpose. Here's what it's actually saying.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: The money an employer pays you for a pay period, after it takes out taxes and anything you've agreed to have deducted. The paper or PDF that comes with it is the pay stub, and it shows every deduction line by line.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone employed by someone else. Self-employed people get paid differently (invoices, no withholding), which is why their taxes work differently too.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: It doesn't, but the companies around it do: payroll providers charge your employer, and some "get paid early" apps charge you a fee or tip to advance money you've already earned.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Not reading the stub. Errors in withholding, missed hours, or a benefit deduction you never signed up for are common and go unnoticed for months.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: How often am I paid? What does each deduction line mean? Is this a W-2 job (employer withholds taxes) or 1099 work (I owe them myself)?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: A $25-an-hour job does not put $1,000 in the bank for a 40-hour week. Here's where the rest went.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Gross pay is what you earned before anything is taken out. Net pay is what actually lands in your account. The difference is taxes and deductions.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Everyone who gets a paycheck, and everyone who's ever been surprised that a $25/hour job doesn't put $1,000 in the bank for a 40-hour week.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Nothing directly. But job offers, loan applications, and rent screens all use gross, while your actual budget runs on net. Mixing them up is how people overcommit.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Budgeting on the gross number. For most people net is roughly 70 to 80% of gross, depending on state and benefits.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's my net per paycheck? Which deductions are required (taxes) and which did I choose (retirement, insurance)?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: A big tax refund feels like a bonus. It's an interest-free loan you gave the government.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Money your employer sends to the government on your behalf out of each paycheck: federal income tax, Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), together called FICA, and state income tax where it applies. The W-4 form you filled out when hired tells them how much to take.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Every W-2 employee. It's not optional.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The government doesn't profit, but over-withholding means you lend it money interest-free all year and get it back as a refund. Under-withholding means a bill, sometimes with a penalty, in April.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Treating a big refund as a bonus. It was your money all along. The reverse risk is a surprise tax bill after a second job or a side gig with no withholding.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What did I put on my W-4, and has my situation changed (marriage, second job, kids)? Does my state have income tax?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Banks pay $300 bonuses for direct deposit. Here's why it's worth that much to them.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Your employer sends pay electronically into a bank account instead of handing you a check. You give them a routing number and an account number once.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Nearly everyone with a bank account. Many employers require it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Banks love it: a steady deposit is why they offer "$300 bonus with direct deposit" and why fee waivers often depend on it. The bank earns by lending out the money that sits there.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Low. The main one is splitting it wrong or forgetting to update it after changing banks.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Can I split it between two accounts (say, checking and savings)? Does my bank waive fees if a deposit comes in?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: Your checking account is a hallway, not a room. Money that lives there earns nothing.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: The bank account money moves through: pay comes in, bills and purchases go out. Comes with a debit card. It's built for spending, not for growing money, so most pay little or no interest.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone who gets paid and pays bills. It's the base account most people open first.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Monthly maintenance fees (often waived with a minimum balance or direct deposit), ATM fees, overdraft fees, and the interest the bank earns lending out your balance while paying you close to nothing.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Fees that add up quietly, and keeping a large balance here where it earns nothing while prices rise.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What's the monthly fee and exactly what waives it? Which ATMs are free? What happens if I spend more than I have?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The $35 fee for having $4 in your account.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Spending more than is in your checking account. The bank either declines the transaction or covers it and charges an overdraft fee, often around $35 per occurrence. Several large banks dropped the fee in 2021 and 2022 and others cut it to about $10; many still charge the full amount.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Nobody on purpose. It happens most to people living paycheck to paycheck, which is why it's been the subject of so much regulation.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The fee itself. Overdraft and NSF fees ran about $5.8 billion in 2023, down from $12.6 billion in 2019. A federal rule capping the fee at $5 at large banks was finalized in December 2024 and repealed by Congress in May 2025, so the fee is back to whatever each bank sets. "Overdraft protection" is a product you opt into that covers the shortfall from a linked account, sometimes for a smaller fee.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Several fees in one day from small purchases. Some banks have reordered transactions largest-first, which triggers more overdrafts.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: Am I opted in to overdraft coverage, or will the card just decline? What's the fee, and is there a daily cap? Can I link savings as a backstop instead?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: The only money idea with nobody selling it.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: Cash kept separate from spending money, meant for things like a car repair, a medical bill, or a gap between jobs. It's a concept, not a product: it usually lives in a savings account.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone whose income could stop or whose expenses could spike, which is nearly everyone. People without one tend to end up on credit cards or overdraft when the surprise comes.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: Nothing. This is one of the few ideas in money with no one selling it. (Banks do benefit when it sits in a low-rate account; see High-yield savings.)

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Raiding it for non-emergencies, so it's gone when needed. The opposite risk is keeping far more than needed in cash while it loses buying power to inflation.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What would I actually need to cover if income stopped? How many months of that feels like enough for my situation? Where can it sit so it's reachable in a day or two but not reachable by my debit card?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.

hook: A budget isn't a diet. It's a map of where the money already goes.

fields.label: What it is
fields.text: A plan for where each paycheck goes before it arrives: bills, saving, spending. Any method works if you look at it monthly. The common ones are a fixed split (needs, wants, saving), giving every dollar a job, or just tracking what left the account last month and deciding what to change.

fields.label: Who ends up using it
fields.text: Anyone whose money runs out before the month does, and anyone who has no idea what they spent last month. That's most people the first time they try it.

fields.label: How it makes money off you
fields.text: The idea is free. The apps around it are not: budgeting apps charge monthly fees or sell you the products they show next to your spending. A spreadsheet or your bank's own category view does the same job for nothing.

fields.label: What goes wrong
fields.text: Making one so detailed it dies in week two. Budgeting on gross pay instead of net. Treating it as a one-time setup instead of a monthly check. Forgetting the once-a-year bills that land all at once.

fields.label: What to ask
fields.text: What did I actually spend last month, by category? Which of those are fixed and which did I choose? What's the one category I'd change first? When will I look at this again?

outro: Educational only. Not investment, tax, or legal advice, and not personalized to you.
